content: 1. Three Italian hospitals implemented the World Health Organization's SARS alert system to manage the outbreak effectively. 2. Tan CC highlighted critical lessons learned from the SARS epidemic in Singapore, emphasizing the importance of rapid response and containment strategies. 3. Olsen SJ and colleagues investigated family clustering of avian influenza A (H5N1), providing insights into transmission dynamics within households. 4. Garner JS developed guidelines for isolation precautions in hospitals, as outlined by the Hospital Infection Control Practices Advisory Committee. 5. Gopalakrishna G and colleagues studied the transmission of SARS in hospital settings and the effectiveness of containment measures. 6. Hammond B et al. examined the impact of hand sanitizer use on absenteeism in elementary schools, demonstrating its role in reducing illness-related absences. 7. Luby SP and colleagues conducted a randomized controlled trial to assess the effect of handwashing on child health, showing significant health benefits. 8. Lai MY, Cheng PK, and Lim WW explored the survival of the SARS coronavirus under various conditions, contributing to understanding its environmental stability. 9. Reynolds MG and colleagues identified factors associated with nosocomial SARS-CoV transmission among healthcare workers in Hanoi, Vietnam, during the 2003 outbreak. 10. Fowler RA et al. analyzed the transmission of SARS during intubation and mechanical ventilation, highlighting the risks associated with aerosol-generating procedures. 11. Scales DC and colleagues reported on illness among intensive care staff following brief exposure to SARS, emphasizing the need for stringent infection control measures. 12. Patrozou E and Mermel LA reviewed whether influenza transmission occurs from asymptomatic individuals or before symptom onset, with implications for public health strategies. 13. Donnelly CA et al. studied the serial intervals and temporal distribution of secondary infections within households during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, providing recommendations for influenza control. 14. Hall CB and Douglas RG Jr. investigated nosocomial influenza infections as a cause of intercurrent fevers in infants, underscoring the importance of hospital infection control. 15. Sato M et al. examined viral shedding in children with influenza infections treated with neuraminidase inhibitors, contributing to understanding treatment efficacy. 16. Chan KH and colleagues detected SARS coronavirus in patients with suspected SARS, aiding in diagnostic advancements. 17. Bloomfield SF proposed a risk-based approach to home hygiene, emphasizing targeted interventions to reduce infection risks. 18. Rheinbaben F et al. conducted experiments using bacteriophage phiX174 as a model virus to study virus transmission via contact in household settings. 19. Tang CS and Wong CY analyzed predictors of health behaviors and the effect of community prevention measures during a SARS outbreak in Hong Kong. 20. Chemaly RF et al. retrospectively studied respiratory viral infections in adults with hematologic malignancies and stem cell transplant recipients, highlighting the vulnerability of immunocompromised patients. 21. Kallander K et al. evaluated home and community management of acute respiratory infections in children across eight Ugandan districts, demonstrating the potential for community-based interventions. 22. Richards DA et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial on home management of mild to moderately severe community-acquired pneumonia, showing its feasibility and effectiveness. 23. Quinlan B et al. gathered feedback from healthcare workers, patients, and families on restrictive visitor policies, providing insights into balancing infection control and patient care. 24. Lee NE et al. shared experiences from mobile SARS containment teams in Laos, Taiwan, and Thailand, highlighting infection control practices during the 2003 outbreak. 25. Mukhopadhyay A et al. reported on a SARS case involving a hospital visitor and her intensivist, emphasizing the importance of visitor screening and infection control. 26. Melnyk BM et al. demonstrated the positive effects of parent empowerment programs on the mental health and coping outcomes of critically ill children and their mothers. 27. Saunders RP et al. evaluated family-centered care practices in neonatal intensive care units, identifying opportunities for improvement. 28. Griffin T discussed the principles of family-centered care in neonatal intensive care units, emphasizing the importance of family involvement in patient care. 29. Chaovavanich A et al. documented early containment efforts of SARS at the Bamrasnaradura Institute in Thailand, showcasing the effectiveness of rapid response measures. 30. Svoboda T et al. analyzed public health measures implemented in Toronto to control the spread of SARS during the outbreak, providing valuable lessons for future epidemics. 31. The World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidance on the transport of infectious substances for 2007–2008, ensuring safe handling and transportation practices. 32. Jahrling P et al. outlined triage and management protocols for accidental laboratory exposures to biosafety level-3 and -4 agents, emphasizing the importance of preparedness. 33. Lim PL et al. reported on a laboratory-acquired SARS case, highlighting the need for stringent biosafety measures in research settings. 34. Alpat SN et al. investigated whether pneumatic sample transport systems could act as carriers for microorganisms, raising concerns about potential contamination risks. 35. The WHO published laboratory biosafety guidelines for handling specimens suspected of containing avian influenza A virus, ensuring safe diagnostic practices. 36. The WHO also released guidelines for the collection of human specimens for laboratory diagnosis of avian influenza infections, standardizing procedures for accurate testing. 37. The WHO Laboratory Biosafety Manual (third edition) provided comprehensive guidance on biosafety practices in laboratory settings. 38. Dey P et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial to promote influenza vaccination uptake among healthcare workers, demonstrating strategies to increase vaccination rates. 39. Dolan GP et al. evaluated the impact of vaccinating healthcare workers to protect high-risk patients from acute respiratory diseases, supporting vaccination campaigns. 40. Lester RT et al. assessed the use, effectiveness, and attitudes toward influenza vaccines among hospital staff, identifying barriers to vaccination. 41. Davis MM et al. highlighted the role of influenza vaccination as secondary prevention for cardiovascular disease, providing evidence for its broader health benefits. 42. Cox S et al. studied hospitalizations for respiratory illnesses among pregnant women during influenza season, emphasizing the need for targeted prevention measures. 43. Buchbinder N et al. successfully managed a sudden outbreak of H1N1 influenza in a pediatric hematology and oncology unit, demonstrating effective containment strategies. 44. Stein A et al. reported on H1N1 infections in very-low-birth-weight infants, providing insights into managing influenza in vulnerable populations. 45. Grund S et al. documented an outbreak of H1N1 influenza in a hospital ward for immunocompromised patients, highlighting the challenges of infection control in such settings. 46. Cunha BA et al. shared lessons learned from a nosocomial H1N1 pneumonia case, emphasizing the importance of early recognition and intervention. 47. Krumkamp R et al. modeled the impact of public health interventions on controlling SARS spread, providing evidence for the effectiveness of various strategies. 48. Yen MY et al. described Taiwan's traffic control bundle, which successfully eliminated nosocomial SARS transmission among healthcare workers. 49. Yen MY et al. quantitatively evaluated infection control models to prevent nosocomial SARS transmission, offering insights for improving healthcare worker safety. 50. Meredith LS et al. proposed a framework for addressing the psychological consequences of patient surges during large-scale disasters, emphasizing mental health preparedness. 51. Aiello A et al. developed resilience training programs for hospital workers in anticipation of an influenza pandemic, enhancing their ability to cope with crises. 52. Yu IT et al. investigated why SARS outbreaks occurred in some hospital wards but not others, identifying factors influencing transmission risk. 53. Lloyd-Smith JO et al. explored strategies to curtail SARS transmission within communities and hospitals, providing recommendations for outbreak control. 54. Kuster SP et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the incidence of influenza among healthy adults and healthcare workers, highlighting occupational risks. 55. Ng ANM and Lai CKY reviewed the effectiveness of seasonal influenza vaccination in healthcare workers, supporting its role in reducing disease transmission. 56. Hall CB and Douglas RG studied the modes of transmission of respiratory syncytial virus, contributing to understanding its spread in healthcare settings. 57. Tsai MC et al. assessed the impact of a SARS outbreak on a hospital in Taiwan, providing lessons for managing future epidemics. 58. Tran K et al. systematically reviewed aerosol-generating procedures and their associated risks of acute respiratory disease transmission, informing infection control practices. 59. Jordan WS Jr. investigated the mechanism of spread of Asian influenza, contributing to understanding its transmission dynamics. 60. Green-McKenzie J et al. evaluated infection control practices among correctional healthcare workers, identifying factors affecting adherence to guidelines. 61. Moore D et al. examined organizational and individual factors influencing healthcare workers' adherence to infection control guidelines during SARS and other respiratory pathogen outbreaks. 62. Ofner M et al. reported on a cluster of SARS cases among protected healthcare workers in Toronto, highlighting the need for comprehensive infection control measures. 63. Seto WH et al. demonstrated the effectiveness of droplet and contact precautions in preventing nosocomial SARS transmission, supporting their use in outbreak settings. 64. Chia SE et al. evaluated the appropriate use of personal protective equipment among healthcare workers during the SARS outbreak in Singapore, identifying areas for improvement. 65. Rengasamy A et al. reviewed respiratory protection against bioaerosols, identifying research needs to enhance healthcare worker safety. 66. The Institute of Medicine provided guidance on the reusability of face masks during an influenza pandemic, addressing challenges in maintaining protection. 67. Hannum D et al. studied the effect of respirator training on healthcare workers' ability to pass qualitative fit tests, emphasizing the importance of proper training. 68. Varia M et al. investigated a nosocomial SARS outbreak in Toronto, identifying factors contributing to its spread and containment. 69. Lee N et al. documented a major SARS outbreak in Hong Kong, providing insights into its epidemiology and control measures. 70. Chen SK et al. evaluated the effectiveness of single-use masks and respirators in protecting healthcare workers from mycobacterial aerosols, informing equipment selection. 71. McCullough NV et al. studied the collection of bacterial aerosols by respirator and surgical mask filters under varying conditions, contributing to understanding their performance. 72. Ho AS et al. reported on a SARS outbreak among hospital workers in a community hospital in Hong Kong, highlighting the importance of infection control measures. 73. Alfa MJ et al. compared sterilization methods, including ion plasma, vaporized hydrogen peroxide, and ethylene oxide, to determine their effectiveness in healthcare settings.
